titulo.texto: Great Basin and Hammered Copper Cauldrons

frase_gancho.texto: Hand-hammered copper that rings like a bell.

puente_narrativo.texto: From metal we move on to thread. Look for a long, slender garment of fine cloth, its ends finished with fringes knotted by hand into patterns.

guion_corto.texto: These copper pieces come from Santa Clara del Cobre, a town in Michoacán famous for working this metal for centuries. They are pitchers, pots and large vessels, a bright reddish color. Each piece is born from a single lump of copper, which is heated until it glows red and struck with mallets on the anvil, by several people, until it takes shape. No solder or molds are used. Look closely at the surface: it is covered with small round marks, the traces of thousands of hammer blows. These marks are not a flaw: they are the signature of handwork, and they make the metal shine differently with every reflection of light.

guion_largo.texto:
If you close your eyes and listen, you can almost hear the workshop: hammers falling one after another on the metal, like a rhythm. This is how Santa Clara del Cobre sounds, the town in Michoacán where these pieces come from. And perhaps this is how the work of the Purépecha metalsmiths you met in the West Hall sounded: in this region, copper is a craft with a long history.

Each piece is born from a blank, a thick disc of copper that is heated until it glows red in the fire. Then several people, standing in a circle, strike it with heavy mallets on an anvil, one by one and in order, as in a dance. Between blows it is heated again, and the disc is stretched and rounded until it becomes a pitcher, a pot or a large shallow pan. There is no solder and no mold: everything is hammer and patience.

Look closely at the surface. It is covered with thousands of marks, small and regular, which are the traces of the blows. When light falls on them, the metal shines in different ways, like a lake with ripples. These marks are what makes a hammered piece valuable: proof that it was made by hands and not by a machine. Copper also changes over time: at first it is reddish and bright, then it darkens and grows warmer, and if neglected it can become covered with a greenish layer. That is why it is polished and cared for.

How did this tradition come to be here? It is said that in the sixteenth century Bishop Vasco de Quiroga, who sought to improve the lives of the peoples of Michoacán, assigned a craft to each community: guitars to some, pottery to others, copper to others. It is a much-repeated story, and it surely oversimplifies; but what is certain is that the Purépecha were already working copper before the Spaniards arrived, and that today's tradition combines that knowledge with techniques that came during the colonial period.

Look carefully at the vessels. They are large because they are used: in Michoacán, carnitas are cooked in copper pots, which spread the heat evenly. The large shallow pans are used for cooking, for making sweets or for storing water. Copper, besides, is a good conductor of heat, and so it works in the kitchen just as it did in jewelry: because it shines and because it endures.

Copper passes from generation to generation. Every August, the town celebrates a fair dedicated to this craft, and families show their finest pieces. Some workshops today recycle metal from cables and pipes, and others keep working with new copper. The tradition has changed and is still alive, which is the best way for a tradition to last.

Now think about what stands before you. If the pectorals and the bells of Purépecha copper that you saw downstairs were adornment and power, these pieces are the opposite: they are everyday work. The same metal serves the king and the kitchen, and perhaps that is its finest quality.

texto.Region: Santa Clara del Cobre, Uruapan and Pátzcuaro, Michoacán
texto.Technique/Material: Fire-hammered copper and lacquer work on wood (axin grease, chia oil and pigments)
texto.Function: Domestic and industrial utensils, sumptuary vessels and ceremonial basins

texto.pregunta: Myth: Hammered copper from Michoacán is a modern craft with no relation to the past.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The Purépecha were already working copper before the Spaniards arrived. Today’s tradition combines that knowledge with techniques that came during the colonial period.
